title: Battle of Chosin Reservoir (1950): The Frozen Breakthrough
subtitle: Nov 27 – Dec 13, 1950

lines: The night of November 27th, 1950. The Chosin Reservoir, high on North Korea's Kaema Plateau.
Temperatures plunged below minus 30 degrees Celsius, and even the oil in the rifles froze.
Then, from every surrounding mountain, bugles sounded.
The Chinese 9th Army Group, some 120,000 men, had encircled the 1st Marine Division.

bubbles.text:
Cut this one road
and it's over!

scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Marines had only one way out:
a single unpaved mountain road running about 126 kilometers through frozen gorges to the sea.
About 30,000 UN troops, built around one Marine division, against four times as many Chinese.
One of history's most brutal encirclements was about to begin.

callouts.text: Per U.S. records · Chinese strength est. 60,000–120,000

lines: And yet two weeks later,
the Marines reached the sea unbroken, bringing their equipment, their wounded, and even their dead.

visual.text:
Two weeks later,
they brought everyone out

lines: A withdrawal that its commander called not a retreat, but an attack in another direction.
This is the miracle of the frozen gorge: the Battle of Chosin Reservoir.
In October 1950, after the Inchon landing, UN forces were driving north.
Everyone believed the war would be over by Christmas.
Under X Corps, the 1st Marine Division advanced north on the eastern front toward the Yalu River.
Its objective lay deep in the Kaema Plateau, beyond the west side of the Chosin Reservoir.
scenes.label: 7th Marines advance north in cold-weather gear (1950)

lines: The division commander, Major General Oliver Smith, was uneasy about this advance.
His units were being strung out far too thinly along a mountain road.
scenes.label: Oliver P. Smith

lines: He had fought through the bloody island battles of Peleliu and Okinawa in the Pacific War.
He knew better than anyone how dangerous a long column deep in enemy country could be.
Smith deliberately slowed the advance.
He stockpiled supplies at Hagaru-ri, built an airstrip, and left troops to guard every key point on the road.
Lay this road out by altitude, and you can see why it was a trap.
It starts on a plateau over 1,000 meters high, then drops almost straight to the sea past Funchilin Pass.
Sheer mountains on both sides, and a road barely wide enough for one truck.
Block a single pass, and the entire division would be trapped.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: And in those mountains, the Chinese were already hiding.
Song Shilun's 9th Army Group, twelve divisions strong, was waiting for the Marines to come deep enough.
Signs that China had entered the war appeared as early as October.
But UN headquarters judged that no large-scale intervention would come.
scenes.label: First Chinese prisoners taken by ROK forces (Oct 1950)

lines: The night of November 27th.
Chinese troops swarmed the Marine positions at Yudam-ni from every direction.
At the same time, the Chinese cut the road between Hagaru-ri and Koto-ri.
In an instant, the Marines were chopped into isolated islands.

callouts.text: MAIN SUPPLY ROUTE CUT IN 3 PLACES

lines: Worse than the enemy was the cold.
Canteens froze solid, and medics reportedly thawed frozen morphine syrettes in their mouths.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: By night came wave after wave of Chinese attacks; by day, endless cold.
In thin cotton uniforms, the Chinese lost even more men to frostbite.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Chinese soldiers endured the same cold.
Canvas shoes like sneakers, frozen rice balls. Many reportedly froze to death in their foxholes, still gripping their rifles.
scenes.label: Chinese POWs south of Koto-ri in canvas sneakers (Dec 1950)

lines: East of the reservoir, the U.S. Army's 31st Regimental Combat Team was cut off.
Of about 2,500 men, only around 1,050 made it back to Hagaru-ri.
And between Yudam-ni and Hagaru-ri lay Toktong Pass.
Holding it, about 240 men of Fox Company held out, surrounded, for five days and nights.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Wounded in the leg, company commander Captain William Barber kept directing the fight from a stretcher.
Had the pass fallen, the two regiments at Yudam-ni would have lost their way home.
Most of the company was killed or wounded, but Fox Company never gave up the pass.
Captain Barber was later awarded the Medal of Honor, America's highest decoration.
On December 1st, the two Marine regiments at Yudam-ni began their breakout toward Hagaru-ri.
After three days of fighting through snow along the ridgelines, they reached Hagaru-ri.
They loaded their wounded onto trucks and brought out their dead as well.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: At Hagaru-ri, there was the airstrip the Marines had prepared in advance.
Transports shuttled across the frozen runway, flying out more than 4,000 wounded.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: There was even an offer to fly the whole division out.
But Smith refused. They would walk out, and they would not abandon their equipment.
scenes.label: Marines between Yudam-ni and Hagaru-ri (Dec 1950)

lines: It was then that Smith is said to have told reporters:
"We are not retreating. We are merely attacking in another direction."

bubbles.text:
Not a retreat —
attacking in another direction!

scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: Maj. Gen. Oliver Smith · Dec 1950 (as reported)

lines: On December 6th, the Marines left Hagaru-ri for Koto-ri.
All night, Chinese fire poured down from the ridges on both sides of the road.
From Hagaru-ri to Koto-ri was about 18 kilometers.
Getting thousands of vehicles and men through took more than a full day.
scenes.label: 7th Marines just south of Hagaru-ri (Dec 6, 1950)

lines: Overhead, Marine Corsair fighter-bombers hammered the ridgelines without pause.
When the troops below called, they arrived within minutes and dropped napalm.
scenes.label: Corsairs drop napalm, seen from the Hagaru-ri perimeter (Dec 1950)

lines: Then, south of Koto-ri at Funchilin Pass, came the worst news of all.
The Chinese had blown the bridge over the gorge. The road was cut.
scenes.label: Blown bridge at Funchilin Pass (Dec 1950)

lines: The gap was about five meters, above a sheer drop.
Without a bridge, no truck, gun, or wounded man could get across.
The Marines' answer was to drop a bridge from the sky.
On December 7th, eight C-119 transports parachuted 1.3-ton steel bridge sections onto Koto-ri.
scenes.label: Bridge section dropped from a C-119 over Koto-ri (Dec 1950)

lines: One was smashed on landing, and one drifted toward Chinese lines,
but the four sections they needed came down intact.
On December 9th, engineers laid the bridge across the gorge in brutal cold.
At last, the Marines' long column began to cross the chasm.
scenes.label: Treadway bridge in place at Funchilin Pass (Dec 9, 1950)

lines: Meanwhile, the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines, fought through a blizzard to seize Hill 1081 overlooking the bridge.
Its job was to protect the engineers from above.
Even on the way down the pass, they did not leave their dead behind.
They carried their frozen comrades on trucks and on guns as they marched.
scenes.label: Marines between Funchilin Pass and Chinhung-ni (Dec 1950)

lines: On December 11th, the last units reached the plain of Hamhung.
Two weeks after being surrounded, the 1st Marine Division had reached the sea.
How did a surrounded division break through four times its number, and the cold?
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, Smith's slow advance.
Despite pressure from above, he built up supplies, cut an airstrip, and held the road.
Without that preparation, Hagaru-ri could never have become a base for rescue.
Second, support from the air.
Close air support, supply drops, and casualty airlifts.
And a bridge dropped from the sky saved the division.
scenes.label: Supply airdrop at Yudam-ni (Nov 29, 1950)

lines: Third, cohesion and discipline.
The units held formation to the end and never abandoned their comrades.
That discipline kept the column from breaking, even in the grip of fear.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Fourth, the cold hit the Chinese even harder.
Even by Chinese count, combat casualties exceeded 21,000, with over 30,000 more lost to frostbite and other causes.
The 1st Marine Division also lost more than 7,000 men to frostbite and illness, on top of its battle casualties.
The Chinese 9th Army Group was unable to fight for nearly three months afterward.
At Hungnam, the port the Marines had fought to reach, another miracle began.
By December 24th, 105,000 troops and 98,000 refugees had been taken aboard ships.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The freighter SS Meredith Victory alone carried about 14,000 refugees.
It would later be recognized as the greatest rescue ever made by a single ship.
scenes.label: Refugees on the deck of SS Meredith Victory (Dec 1950)

lines: After the last ship sailed, the docks at Hungnam were blown up.
scenes.label: Demolition of Hungnam port (Dec 24, 1950)

lines: Those who came back from Chosin called themselves 'The Chosin Few.'
Across America, memorials to them still stand today.
scenes.label: Chosin Few Memorial dedication

lines: And among the refugees they carried to safety were the parents and grandparents of many Koreans living today.
scenes.label: Hungnam refugees aboard an LST and fishing boats (Dec 1950)

lines: A frozen gorge, and a single road.
Those who walked it to the end were the ones who never left a comrade behind.

items.text: A frozen gorge, a single road
They never left a comrade behind
